label: Approval
title: Human-in-the-Loop Approval
subtitle: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) lets you review and authorise agent actions before they execute. This matters because agents can run shell commands, write files, and make network requests — actions that are difficult or impossible to undo. Enabling approval gives you a checkpoint between what the agent plans to do and what actually happens on your system.

subsections.title: When to Use Approval
subsections.description: Not every agent action carries the same risk. Reading a file or searching the web are low-stakes operations — if the agent reads the wrong document, it just gets incorrect context. But running a shell command, writing to the filesystem, or delegating a large task to another agent can have lasting consequences. A useful rule of thumb: keep approval on during any session where agents have access to file writing or shell execution, especially while you are still learning how a particular agent behaves. Once you trust a tool or workflow, you can set individual tools to auto-approve so they no longer interrupt you.
subsections.mediaCaption: The inline approval strip above the chat input, showing the agent name, the action it wants to take, and the exact parameters it plans to use

subsections.title: Setting Approval Levels
subsections.description: Each tool assigned to an agent can be configured independently. Open an agent's settings and click the configure icon next to any tool to open the Tool Configuration dialog. Inside, you will find a dropdown for each method (sub-action) that tool can perform. There are five levels: Always Approved means the action runs without interruption; Notify shows a notification but does not block execution; Ask pauses execution and requires you to click Approve or Reject before the agent continues — but is auto-approved when Human-in-the-Loop is turned off; Always Ask works like Ask but can never be skipped, so it pauses for your confirmation even when Human-in-the-Loop is off — this is the default for dangerous actions such as shell execution and file deletion; Disabled prevents the agent from using that method entirely. You can use the bulk selector at the top of the dialog to set the same level for all methods at once.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Tool Configuration dialog showing the bulk approval selector and a list of individual methods, each with its own approval level dropdown colour-coded by level

subsections.title: Reviewing a Request
subsections.description: When an agent reaches an action set to Ask, execution pauses and an approval strip appears inline between the chat messages and the text input. The strip shows a warning icon with a badge count of pending requests, the agent name, and navigation arrows so you can cycle through multiple approvals without leaving the conversation. Click the strip or the chevron to expand it and see the full approval card — the agent name, the action it wants to take, a human-readable description, and a code/query preview. Click Approve to let the action proceed. Click Always to approve this action and automatically approve all future requests from the same tool for the rest of the session. Switching Human-in-the-Loop off and back on clears every Always grant made in the session, so those tools ask again. Click Reject to decline the action. Declining a read-only lookup never stops the agent — it continues with whatever results it has. If it retries the same declined call and you decline again, it stops pursuing that lookup; calls to the same tool for other purposes you keep approving remain available. Rejecting an action with side effects (like writing a file or running a command) stops the agent so you can redirect it. You can also swipe horizontally or use the keyboard arrow keys to navigate between multiple pending approvals — the chat automatically scrolls to show where in the conversation the request was made. Once all approvals are handled the strip disappears. The Notifications section in the right sidebar keeps a read-only history of past approvals and their outcomes.
subsections.mediaCaption: The inline approval strip expanded to show a pending request card with Approve, Always, and Reject buttons, plus navigation arrows and a badge showing the total pending count

subsections.title: Running without approval (HITL off)
subsections.description: You can disable Human-in-the-Loop from the approval strip to let agents run without interruption. In this mode methods set to Ask are auto-approved and no approval cards appear for them — useful for trusted, well-tested workflows or batch operations where constant prompts would be impractical. There is one deliberate exception: methods set to Always Ask still pause for your confirmation even with HITL off. This protects the most dangerous actions — shell execution, file deletion, and similar irreversible operations ship as Always Ask by default — so turning HITL off can never silently run them. Methods set to Notify also keep notifying even with HITL off: the notification is informational and never blocks, so you stay aware of those actions without being interrupted. To make a session truly uninterrupted you would also have to lower those methods from Always Ask in each tool's configuration dialog, which is not recommended. To re-enable full oversight at any time, switch HITL back on — doing so also clears every Always grant made in this session, so the tools you waved through start asking again. Keep in mind that with HITL off there is no checkpoint before file writes or other Ask-level actions execute — use this mode only when you understand what the agent will do.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Tool Configuration dialog with the bulk selector set to Always Approved, showing all methods in the list updated to the green Always Approved state

subsections.title: Tool-specific card layouts
subsections.description: Most approval requests show a standard text card: the action, a description, and a parameter preview. Some tools provide a purpose-built layout instead — for example, a command tool can present the exact shell command it wants to run in a clearly formatted block so you can review it at a glance, and a file write, update, or edit shows the target path with the full incoming content (or the before/after replacement for an edit) in a monospace block, rather than reading it out of a generic parameter list. The platform always keeps the Approve, Always, and Reject controls itself, so the layout a tool chooses only changes how the request is presented, never how it is authorised. Tools can only pick from layouts the platform ships; a request with no special layout falls back to the standard text card.
